---
title: "Error Handling in Pipelines"
---

# Error Handling in Pipelines

`Result` in a pipeline is still a `Result`. The choice is what you do with the first `Err`: return it, store it beside the successes, or drop it. Pick one on purpose.

## The concept

`collect::<Result<Vec<T>, E>>()` uses the `FromIterator` implementation for `Result`. The first `Err` becomes the result of `collect`, and the remaining items are not consumed. That is fail-fast. It is not "gather every error".

`?` inside a closure returns from the closure. It does not return from the function that built the closure, unless the closure is not a closure and you are in the function body.

## Recipe 65 — Fail fast: stop at the first error

```rust
fn main() {
    let fields = ["10", "20", "nope", "40"];
    let parsed: Result<Vec<i32>, _> = fields.iter().map(|text| text.parse::<i32>()).collect();
    assert!(parsed.is_err());

    let mut iter = fields.iter().map(|text| text.parse::<i32>());
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(Ok(10)));
    assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(Ok(20)));
    assert!(iter.next().unwrap().is_err());
}
```

The second block shows the items one by one so you can see that `"40"` is never required for the failure. `collect` stops pulling once it has an `Err`.

## Recipe 66 — Collect all errors before reporting

Fail-fast is wrong when the caller should fix every bad row in one pass.

```rust
fn main() {
    let fields = ["10", "nope", "40", "also"];
    let mut values = Vec::new();
    let mut errors = Vec::new();
    for (index, text) in fields.iter().enumerate() {
        match text.parse::<i32>() {
            Ok(n) => values.push(n),
            Err(err) => errors.push(format!("field {index}: {err}")),
        }
    }
    assert_eq!(values, [10, 40]);
    assert_eq!(errors.len(), 2);
}
```

This is a loop because it writes two collections and keeps going. A fold into `(Vec<_>, Vec<_>)` is the same loop with more punctuation. Use the fold if you are already inside a chain and the body stays small. Use the loop when you are explaining the policy to the next reader.

## Recipe 67 — Skip errors silently

```rust
fn main() {
    let fields = ["10", "nope", "40"];
    let values: Vec<i32> = fields.iter().filter_map(|text| text.parse().ok()).collect();
    assert_eq!(values, [10, 40]);
}
```

`.ok()` throws the `ParseIntError` away. Use this for data you have already decided is best-effort. Do not use it for a config file. The missing row is invisible.

## Recipe 68 — Using the ? operator inside closures

`?` works in a closure that returns `Result`. It returns from that closure only.

```rust
fn main() {
    let fields = ["10", "20"];
    let values: Result<Vec<i32>, std::num::ParseIntError> = fields
        .iter()
        .map(|text| {
            let n: i32 = text.parse()?;
            Ok(n + 1)
        })
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(values.unwrap(), [11, 21]);
}
```

This does not compile, and the compiler is right:

```text
fn load(fields: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<i32>, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    let values = fields.iter().map(|text| text.parse::<i32>()?).collect();
    Ok(values)
}
```

The `?` sits in the closure, whose return type would be `i32`, not `Result`. `?` has nothing fallible to return from except that closure. Write `text.parse::<i32>()` without `?`, and let `collect` turn `Result`s into one `Result`. Or write the `?` in the function body inside a `for` loop.

## Recipe 69 — Transforming error types mid-pipeline

`map_err` changes the error and leaves `Ok` values alone. Do it before `collect` so the collected error type matches the function.

```rust
fn main() {
    let fields = ["10", "nope"];
    let values: Result<Vec<i32>, String> = fields
        .iter()
        .map(|text| {
            text.parse::<i32>()
                .map_err(|err| format!("{text:?} is not an integer ({err})"))
        })
        .collect();
    let message = values.unwrap_err();
    assert!(message.contains("nope"));
}
```

`map_err` is lazy in the same way `map` is. It runs when that item is pulled. Fail-fast `collect` pulls through the bad item and stops, so later `map_err` closures do not run.

## Recipe 70 — Building a pipeline that returns Result

Put the pipeline in a function whose return type is the `Result` you want. Inference then fills in `collect`.

```rust
fn temperatures(lines: &str) -> Result<Vec<i32>, String> {
    lines
        .lines()
        .filter(|line| !line.trim().is_empty())
        .map(|line| {
            let field = line.trim();
            field
                .parse::<i32>()
                .map_err(|_| format!("bad temperature {field:?}"))
        })
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    assert_eq!(temperatures("18\n\n21\n").unwrap(), [18, 21]);
    assert!(temperatures("18\nhot\n").is_err());
}
```

Empty lines are filtered before `parse`, so a blank line is not an error. `"hot"` is. The function does not partially apply the good prefix when a later line fails. If the caller needs the prefix, return a struct with both the values and the error. Do not return `Ok` of a short `Vec` and log the rest where nobody looks.
